title: What training supports an adequate procedures defense to failure to prevent foreign bribery?
description: How training supports the adequate procedures defense to the section 70.5A failure to prevent foreign bribery offense, per the Attorney-General's guidance.
shortAnswer: Since 8 September 2024, section 70.5A of the Criminal Code makes a corporation liable if an associate bribes a foreign public official for its benefit, unless it proves it had adequate procedures to prevent bribery. The Attorney-General's Department guidance names communication and training as one of six elements, expecting risk based, role tailored and continuous training for directors, managers, employees and at risk associates, with completion and attendance records.
keyTakeaways: The failure to prevent offense in section 70.5A commenced on 8 September 2024 under the Crimes Legislation Amendment (Combatting Foreign Bribery) Act 2024.
The only offense specific defense is proving adequate procedures were in place (section 70.5A(5)); the corporation bears the legal burden.
The Attorney-General's Department guidance of August 2024 sets six elements, one of which is communication and training.
The guidance says simply asking employees to acknowledge they have read the program is inadequate, and training should be tailored to higher risk roles and reviewed periodically.
The maximum fine is the greatest of 100,000 penalty units, three times the benefit, or 10% of annual turnover when the benefit cannot be determined.
regulator: Attorney-General's Department (policy and guidance); Australian Federal Police (investigation); Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions (prosecution)
appliesTo: Constitutional corporations, including Australian financial and trading corporations and foreign corporations
Bodies corporate incorporated or taken to be registered in a Territory
Directors, managers and employees of those corporations
Associates such as agents, contractors, subsidiaries and others performing services on the corporation's behalf

sections.heading: What is the failure to prevent foreign bribery offense?

blocks.text: Section 70.5A of the [Criminal Code](https://www.legislation.gov.au/C2004A04868/latest/text) makes a body corporate guilty of an offense if an associate bribes a foreign public official, or engages in equivalent conduct overseas, for the profit or gain of the body corporate. Absolute liability applies to key elements, so the company does not need to have known about or authorized the bribe.

The offense was inserted by the Crimes Legislation Amendment (Combatting Foreign Bribery) Act 2024, which received assent on 8 March 2024. The compilation endnotes record that the relevant items of Schedule 1 commenced on 8 September 2024. It applies to constitutional corporations and to bodies corporate incorporated in, or taken to be registered in, a Territory. This page reflects the law and guidance as at September 2026.

"Associate" is defined broadly in section 70.1. According to the [Attorney-General's Department (AGD)](https://www.ag.gov.au/crime/foreign-bribery/foreign-bribery-offences-and-penalties), a person is an associate of a corporation if they are an officer, employee, agent or contractor, a subsidiary, a controlled entity, or otherwise perform services for or on behalf of the corporation. A corporation can be convicted even if the associate has not been convicted.

sections.heading: What is the adequate procedures defense?

blocks.text: The defense is the corporation proving it had adequate procedures designed to prevent its associates from bribing foreign public officials. It is the only offense specific defense to section 70.5A, and the corporation bears a legal burden of proof.

blocks.title: Primary text: Criminal Code, section 70.5A(5)
blocks.text: "Subsection (1) does not apply if the first person proves that the first person had in place adequate procedures designed to prevent: (a) the commission of an offence against section 70.2 by any associate of the first person; and (b) any associate of the first person engaging in conduct outside Australia that, if engaged in in Australia, would constitute an offence against section 70.2."

Section 70.5B required the Minister to publish guidance on the steps a body corporate can take, and the AGD published its [Guidance on adequate procedures to prevent the commission of foreign bribery](https://www.ag.gov.au/crime/publications/guidance-adequate-procedures-prevent-commission-foreign-bribery) on 28 August 2024. The guidance is not a legislative instrument, and whether procedures were adequate is ultimately decided by a court case by case.

The guidance makes two points that shape training design. First, "the mere existence of anti-bribery controls will not be sufficient": the corporation must show the procedures were adequate. Second, controls should be proportionate to the corporation's circumstances, including the scale and location of its activities and the nature and level of risk identified, so higher risk means more training.

sections.heading: Where does training sit in the AGD guidance?

blocks.text: Training is the fourth of six elements in the AGD guidance, and it depends on the others, especially the risk assessment. The six elements are:

items: Fostering a control environment to prevent foreign bribery.

blocks.text: The guidance says frequency and content of communications and training should be proportionate to the bribery risks faced, and that training should cover how employees and associates are expected to respond to bribe solicitation and where to report concerns. It links reporting to whistleblower protections under the Corporations Act, which is covered in [whistleblower policy training requirements](/regulations/whistleblower-policy-training-requirements).

blocks.title: AGD guidance, section 4.1
blocks.text: "Simply asking employees to acknowledge that they have read and understood the anti-bribery compliance program is inadequate."

sections.heading: What does the AGD guidance say training should do?

blocks.text: The guidance says training should be tailored to the needs identified in the risk assessment and designed to mitigate those risks. It lists the following characteriztics, which work well as a design checklist.

items: Be provided to the corporation's directors, managers and employees.
Be provided to other associates, such as agents, contractors or suppliers, considered at risk of foreign bribery.
Be accessible in different formats and languages as necessary.
Cover general and sector specific bribery risks and the corporation's anti-bribery compliance program, including all related policies.
Be tailored to employees in higher risk functions, such as purchasing and contracting.
Include case studies or real life scenarios relevant to the business.
Be included in induction for new employees.
Undergo periodic review so it addresses contemporary bribery risks.
Be continuous, and integrated into the business environment as much as possible.

blocks.text: The guidance adds that corporations should keep training completion records and participant attendance lists as good practice, and should take a risk based approach to training third parties. Its case study suggests specialized training for high exposure employees on how bribe demands typically arise and how to resist them, including the message that employees will not be penalized for refusing to pay bribes.

sections.heading: How can training evidence support the defense?

blocks.text: Evidence should show that training followed the risk assessment, reached the people and associates who carry the most risk, and changed what they could do. The table below is an illustrative mapping; it is not legal advice and does not guarantee a court will find procedures adequate.

blocks.text: Evidence of this kind is easier to produce when obligations, outcomes and records are linked from the start. See [how to map training to compliance obligations](/guides/how-to-map-training-to-compliance-obligations) and [how to evidence training effectiveness to a regulator](/guides/how-to-evidence-training-effectiveness-to-a-regulator). A [policy attestation](/glossary/policy-attestation) can form part of the record, but the AGD guidance is explicit that acknowledgement alone is not enough.

sections.heading: What are the penalties and who enforces the offense?

blocks.text: The section 70.5A offense is indictable and carries a maximum fine equal to the greatest of three amounts. There is no imprisonment because the offense applies to bodies corporate.

items: Three times the value of the benefit obtained, where the court can determine it.
Where the benefit cannot be determined, 10% of the corporation's annual turnover in the 12 months ending at the end of the month the conduct occurred or began.

blocks.text: Extended geographical jurisdiction (category A) applies. The AGD explains that the offense covers conduct by associates inside Australia for Australian and foreign corporations, and conduct outside Australia for Australian corporations. The [AGD sets whole of government policy](https://www.ag.gov.au/crime/foreign-bribery/agency-roles-and-responsibilities), the Australian Federal Police investigates, and the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions prosecutes. The AGD has held public consultation for a statutory review of the 2024 Act, with consultation closing on 10 September 2026, so further changes are possible.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry links bribery risks from the risk assessment to defined learning outcomes, audiences and assessment points, including associate training, so the corporation can show why each group received the training it did. Content versions and review triggers are recorded, which supports the periodic review element. See [audit evidence](/platform/audit-evidence) and [financial services](/industries/financial-services).

faqs.q: Does the failure to prevent offense apply to small companies?
faqs.a: Yes. It applies to constitutional corporations regardless of size. The AGD guidance says it is reasonable to expect corporations of all sizes to put in place appropriate and proportionate controls, so a small company with limited foreign exposure can use simpler training, but failing to take any steps would likely mean procedures are inadequate.

faqs.q: Do contractors and agents need anti-bribery training?
faqs.a: The guidance says training should be provided to associates such as agents, contractors or suppliers considered at risk of foreign bribery, using a risk based approach. In some cases the third party may provide its own training; in others the corporation's internal training may be suitable.

No interval is set in the Criminal Code or the guidance. The guidance says frequency should be proportionate to the bribery risks faced, that training should be continuous and periodically reviewed, and that it should form part of induction. Higher risk roles would reasonably receive more frequent and specialized training.

faqs.q: Are facilitation payments still a defense?
faqs.a: Section 70.4 retains a facilitation payment defense to the individual offense in section 70.2, subject to conditions including a record keeping requirement. The AGD recommends resisting facilitation payments, which are often illegal overseas, so training should explain the company's own policy clearly.

factCheck.claim: Section 70.5A(1) offence: body corporate whose associate commits or would commit a s 70.2 offence for its profit or gain; absolute liability applies to specified elements; conviction possible without conviction of the associate.

Section 70.5A(5) adequate procedures exception with legal burden on the defendant (s 13.4); s 70.5A(6) penalty is greatest of 100,000 penalty units, 3 times the benefit, or 10% of annual turnover; s 70.5A(8) indictable; s 70.5B requires the Minister to publish guidance.
Crimes Legislation Amendment (Combatting Foreign Bribery) Act 2024 (No. 5, 2024) assent 8 March 2024; Schedule 1 items 1 to 10 commenced 8 September 2024 (Criminal Code endnotes).
AGD guidance published 28 August 2024 sets six elements including communication and training.

Guidance section 4: frequency and content proportionate to risk; asking employees to acknowledge the program is inadequate; training list including directors, at risk associates, higher risk functions, induction, periodic review, continuous; keep completion records and attendance lists.

Associate includes officer, employee, agent, contractor, subsidiary, controlled entity or a person otherwise performing services for the corporation; adequate procedures is the only offence specific defence to s 70.5A.
AGD statutory review of the 2024 Act open for consultation closing 10 September 2026.
AGD is responsible for whole of government foreign bribery policy; AFP investigates offences including bribery of a foreign public official.
